item1_measured_vs_inferred_ruling.instruction: Check ADR-019/020's claims trace to what the spike ACTUALLY measured, specifically the 'Path C is safe' (user-scope MCP registrations survive uninstall) claim.
item1_measured_vs_inferred_ruling.claim_location: hld.md ADR-020, lines 730-734: 'Path C is safe, and it is an unintended benefit of ADR-019... Because registrations are written at user scope rather than bundled in a plugin .mcp.json, they survive plugin uninstall.'
item1_measured_vs_inferred_ruling.what_the_spike_actually_measured: plugin_schema_spike.md Item 4 measured two things: (a) the spike's OWN throwaway plugin's bundled .mcp.json server was explicitly confirmed NOT merged into settings.json's mcpServers key at all -- 'it stays scoped to the plugin and is tracked separately' via installed_plugins.json/the plugin manifest system (Item 3). (b) The Final Verification section confirms 'the 5 hook registrations and 25 pre-existing mcpServers entries are byte-for-byte identical to baseline' after the full install/uninstall/marketplace-remove/prune cycle -- but these 25 entries PRE-DATE the spike; they were never written BY any plugin command.
item1_measured_vs_inferred_ruling.gap: The spike never created an entry inside settings.json's mcpServers key via a plugin-owned command (the exact mechanism register-mcp would use, since register-mcp does not exist yet) and then tested whether THAT entry survives uninstall. It only observed that (i) pre-existing, unrelated entries survive, and (ii) uninstall's settings.json footprint is limited to enabledPlugins/extraKnownMarketplaces. Extrapolating from 'uninstall does not touch mcpServers at all' to 'a register-mcp-created mcpServers entry will therefore also survive' is a REASONABLE inference (same key, same passive-non-touch mechanism) but it IS an inference, not a direct measurement -- register-mcp's write path was never exercised by the spike.
item1_measured_vs_inferred_ruling.ruling: INFERRED, NOT MEASURED. The inference is well-reasoned (structural analogy: register-mcp writes to the same mcpServers key that uninstall was shown not to touch at all) and is probably correct, but the HLD presents it with zero hedging as a flatly measured fact ('Path C is safe... they survive plugin uninstall'), used as load-bearing justification for ADR-020's Path C row ('None needed -- see below' in the interception-point table). Per the instructions, reasoned architectural judgement is not hallucination when its inputs are traceable -- but here the INPUT ITSELF is misrepresented: the document does not say 'inferred from Item 4's finding that the uninstall mechanism does not touch the mcpServers key at all' -- it says the registrations 'survive plugin uninstall' as accomplished fact.
item1_measured_vs_inferred_ruling.why_load_bearing: ADR-020's three-layer control scheme explicitly assigns Path C 'None needed' specifically because Path C is asserted safe. If the inference is wrong (e.g., a future Claude Code version treats plugin-command-written mcpServers entries differently from pre-existing ones, or register-mcp's implementation is later found to write through a different code path), Path C would need the same PREVENT/DETECT treatment given to Paths A and B, and nothing currently plans for that.
item1_measured_vs_inferred_ruling.recommended_fix: Add one clause: 'This is inferred from Item 4's finding that uninstall does not touch settings.json's mcpServers key at all (verified only for pre-existing entries and the spike's own non-mcpServers-key bundled server) -- register-mcp's own write path was not itself exercised by the spike. Recommend a targeted re-test once register-mcp exists: register via the real command, uninstall, confirm survival.'

item5_nfr3_survival_argument_ruling.instruction: Verify the claim that ADR-011's no-dual-write rule means MCP opt-in (ADR-019) did not break NFR-3, against ADR-011's actual text.
item5_nfr3_survival_argument_ruling.claim_location: hld.md SS9 'Cross-NFR interaction check' table, lines 1233-1243, NFR-3 row; corroborated by sa_defence.json ba_findings/cross-NFR note line 191
item5_nfr3_survival_argument_ruling.adr011_actual_text_checked: ADR-011 defect 2 (verified in an earlier pass, re-confirmed present this pass): 'Checkpoint and progress must not become a dual write ... The offset/progress record must be committed in the same transaction as the state it describes ... This design takes the first option: progress is a field of the checkpoint record, and the MCP progress tool is a projection of it, not an independent writer.' ADR-011's Chosen section separately names CheckpointManager (in-process, triggered by core/step_decorator.py at every step boundary) as the sole writer, entirely independent of any MCP call.
item5_nfr3_survival_argument_ruling.reasoning_check: Holds exactly. NFR-3's actual AC ('kill mid-pipeline; resume picks up at the correct step') depends only on CheckpointManager's step-boundary writes, which are engine-internal function calls inside step_decorator.py -- not MCP tool invocations, and therefore not gated by whether the user has run register-mcp. mcp-post-tool-tracker (which DOES become opt-in under ADR-019) is, per ADR-011's own explicit design choice, a read-side PROJECTION of already-committed checkpoint state, used only for the finer-grained per-tool-call progress QUERY surface -- a distinct, lesser capability from crash-recovery correctness. The hld.md table's conclusion ('Crash recovery is therefore unaffected ... only the query surface is [affected]') is a precise, correctly-scoped consequence of ADR-011's actual mechanism, not an overclaim.
item5_nfr3_survival_argument_ruling.cross_document_consistency: hld.md's SS9 table and sa_defence.json's independent restatement (line 191: 'A user who never registers MCP loses the query surface, not crash recovery') use materially identical reasoning and reach the same conclusion, both correctly traceable to ADR-011's text.
item5_nfr3_survival_argument_ruling.verdict: REASONING HOLDS -- NFR-3 genuinely did not break, and the document correctly shows its work rather than asserting the conclusion.
